bbc_card_1.headline: AI staff 'genuinely frightened' for humanity's future, ex-Anthropic researcher tells BBC
bbc_card_1.description: Jacob Coxon tells the BBC that there's a strong chance AI could end humanity if the rate of development is not reined in.
bbc_card_1.article_content:
An AI researcher who quit Anthropic has told the BBC that people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

Jacob Coxon spoke to the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg on Saturday about his viral resignation post in which he raised concerns about out-of-control artificial intelligence.

"I believe that if we don't slow down at the current rate of progress, there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future," he said.

His resignation comes amid growing safety concerns in the industry, including from his former boss, Anthropic head Dario Amodei, who in an essay argued for development to slow down.

The 27-year-old Coxon - who worked at OpenAI before joining Anthropic - welcomed the suggestion of a slowdown from Amodei but said it would need to be co-ordinated with China.

"The people who work at these companies are completely serious when they ask for regulation because they find themselves trapped in a race. And they're scared of the outcomes of that race," he told Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg.

"Sam Altman and Elon Musk have agreed that this is a great idea. But I think there'll need to be some sort of co-ordinated slowdown with China if we're going to avoid a race at an international scale."

The hardest question to answer, according to Coxon, was what an AI apocalypse would look like.

One of the risks outlined in Amodei's comments was of a swarm of bots acting like a supercomputer that could take over the internet.

Coxon said this scenario could be realistic in six months to a year.

In response to Coxon's departure, an Anthropic spokesperson told BBC News: "We have always been transparent that AI will bring both enormous benefits and unprecedented risks.

"To address these risks, we continue to build models with some of the strongest safeguards in the industry."

The firm has been a pioneer in studying how AI models work, the spokesperson added. It was the first to publish a framework for mitigating the risks posed by their development - and it also "aggressively" tests its models and publishes the findings to aid scrutiny and prevent incidents of "AI misalignment".

"This work is also why we believe the world would benefit from the industry adopting a lawful, verifiable way to work together to pace how we release powerful models," they said.

In Amodei's essay, called We Must Pace the Frontier and published on Saturday, he proposed a three-point plan that included independent monitoring of AI models as they are developed, industry-wide regulation and global regulation.

Anthropic and OpenAI are reportedly preparing for potentially record-setting initial public offerings.

Industry figures have suggested comments about the perils and power of AI may be designed to generate hype. Other critics say Anthropic has been trying to trigger a regulatory push to block competition, leaving it and OpenAI with a duopoly.

Coxon's views have also been questioned by the CEO of the AI platform Hugging Face, Clement Delangue.

"Sorry, but asking Jacob about AI extinction risk is like asking your AC guy about climate change," he wrote on X. "Not saying it's necessarily uninteresting or wrong per se but let's keep things in perspective."

After Amodei's, however, Delangue offered to help be a part of the potential solutions proposed by the Anthropic boss.

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang also discussed Coxon's comments at a conference hosted by the investment bank Goldman Sachs last week, multiple people in the group told the BBC. They said he dismissed them as untrue.

Huang has previously said the notion that AI was "going to be the end of humanity" is "complete nonsense".

And while he may have a business interest in an AI boom - Nvidia builds chips that power AI systems - his comments reflect a growing backlash in Silicon Valley to the existential warnings from current and former staffers.

Coxon said his peers feared the danger could even arrive in the next two years.

He said staff at AI firms were "planning what to do with their lives and thinking about the impacts of their work", while some were "considering buying land somewhere because they're so scared of the instability as a result of rapid AI progress".

"They all keep this in their head on a daily basis while working on the technology."

But Coxon did have some optimism about the future of AI, telling the BBC that the people researching the technology "genuinely want to see the upside" of things like "solving diseases and improving everyone's lives" with AI.

His comments about AI have been shared millions of times on social media, with Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger responding on X that he agreed with Coxon.

"We really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade," Hubinger said.

Leading figures in the AI field have been raising the alarm about the safety threat the tech poses for years, with the heads of OpenAI, Google Deepmind and Anthropic saying as much in 2023.

These warnings have become louder in recent weeks, as evidence emerges that firms may be struggling to control the technology.

bbc_card_2.headline: They lost their jobs after posting about Charlie Kirk, but some have no regrets
bbc_card_2.description: Some people fired in the wake of Kirk's assassination have won big settlements from employers, others have had to start over from scratch.
bbc_card_2.article_content:
In September 2025, Gerald Bourguet felt he was finally living his dream life: he and his wife had bought a house with a pool, they had just welcomed a baby boy, and he was writing about professional men's basketball as his full-time job.

But all of that changed after he made a series of online posts critical of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk hours after he was fatally shot on 10 September, while speaking on the campus of Utah Valley University.

In the posts, Bourguet described Kirk as an "evil man" and suggested he had dedicated his life to hateful causes. He also criticised Kirk's supporters saying they had not been vocal about school shootings.

"I had seen the way that people were talking about this person - kind of eulogising him and lionising him and it bothered me based on a lot of the things that he had said," Bourguet told the BBC.

Kirk, who founded Christian youth organisation Turning Point USA, was a divisive figure in US politics. For many on the political right, he was charismatic and had a unique skill in making conservative ideas appeal to young people. But for his opponents, his comments on a large swathe of issues from race to immigration, gun control and gender identity were deeply offensive.

Screenshots of Bourguet's critical posts went viral quickly. He was fired from his job, his address was exposed online, and he began receiving threatening text messages, he said. Concerned for their safety, the family fled the state with their four-month-old. They returned months later to sell the house and permanently relocated.

A year later, he says he doesn't regret what he said, but acknowledged: "My life will never be the same after this".

"At age 35, I am having to start over in a lot of respects… I wouldn't wish this on my worst enemy," Bourguet said from his new location, which the BBC agreed not to disclose.

PHNX Sports, Bourguet's former employer, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Bourguet was one of hundreds fired or disciplined over critical comments of Kirk after his death. While some of those who have lost their jobs have been reinstated or received restitution - sometimes in the millions - others like Bourguet have had to rebuild from scratch.

In the aftermath of Kirk's assassination, most people kept their feelings to themselves, or shared them with close friends.

But on polarised social media, people rushed to laude, or denounce, the controversial activist. Some called the criticisms, posted hours after his death, tasteless. But others called for swift action, arguing they were callous, mocking, and could even incite further violence.

Laura Loomer, an influential right-wing commentator with nearly 2 million followers on X, warned Kirk's critics to "prepare to have your whole future professional aspirations ruined".

The push for punishment also came from the highest levels of US government.

"When you see someone celebrating Charlie's murder, call them out," Vice-President JD Vance said days after the assassination. "And hell, call their employer," he added.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told the BBC: "Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible."

Critics on the left said there was a difference between criticism of Kirk and celebrating his death. Some accused these conservative leaders of hypocrisy, as many had previously bemoaned the rise of "cancel culture" – where people who voice controversial opinions face severe consequences at work and socially.

"Cancel culture can be good, it's bad when it's applied in the wrong ways," Jordan Pace, a Republican member of the South Carolina House of Representatives, told the BBC. "If you are someone who celebrates political assassinations and the murder of an innocent man with two young children in a way that many people did, then yeah, that's an appropriate way for society to function, to shame those people."

Pace had previously called for defunding universities in his state if they didn't take actions against employees who made comments about Kirk. One of his posts was re-shared by US President Donald Trump.

Across the nation, some employers – private and public – acted swiftly to the pressure campaign. Reliable figures on the number of people fired or disciplined are hard to come by, but a Reuters tally last November found more than 600 instances. It is likely an under-count because not all cases received national or local press attention.

The specific actions that led to these disciplinary decisions run the gamut. In Tennessee, anthropology professor Tamar Shirinian was suspended and later fired for a Facebook comment saying "the world is better off" without Kirk.

A Delta Air Lines flight attendant was fired after posting "good riddance" in response to Kirk's killing. Office Depot supply store fired an employee for refusing to serve a customer who had wanted to print flyers for a Kirk vigil. Delta Air Lines declined to comment. Office Depot did not respond to a request for comment.

Others were disciplined even if they did not make any direct comments about Kirk or his death. Darren Michael, a theatre professor in Tennessee, was fired after he posted a screenshot of a news article from 2023, that covered Kirk's controversial speech on gun control. In the article, Kirk is quoted saying protecting citizens' rights to own guns was worth it even if it led to some gun deaths every year.

Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission fired biologist Brittney Brown after she reposted a meme that also satirised Kirk's position on gun violence in light of his own shooting.

"I was absolutely gutted," Brown said about her firing to the BBC. "It was like the entire world just completely flipped on its head in a moment."

In the year since Kirk's killing, dozens of lawsuits have been filed across the country by people fired for their comments about the activist, arguing their terminations violated their rights to free speech. The suits have led to substantial pay outs in some cases.

Brown agreed to a $485,000 (£355,000) financial settlement – about 12 times Brown's annual salary.

Darren Michael was reinstated by the Austin Peay State University and in January, the school agreed to pay him $500,000 to settle legal claims. The school did not respond to a request for comment.

In the largest settlement reviewed by the BBC, the University of Tennessee agreed to pay $1.9m to resolve a lawsuit brought by anthropologist Tamar Shirinian, over her "better off" comment. As part of the settlement, she will not be reinstated and has agreed not to reapply for future positions at the school.

Recently, an arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire, with back pay, opinion journalist Karen Attiah, who was fired for her online posts that said in part she was not going to engage in "performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence".

Several other lawsuits remain pending, the BBC found.

Most of the legal actions have been pursued by employees of government institutions, or unionised workers, who have some free-speech protections.

But in the US, most private sector employees work under "at-will" contracts, which means they can be can be fired without reason.

Even those who have scored some victories don't see it as a win.

"All I wanted was my job back," biologist Brown said. "How much taxpayer money did they waste on this when I barely made $40,000 a year? So no, it does not feel like justice."

Shirinian told the BBC she too had wanted to return to her job but felt a legal case could be a lengthy affair.

"I took a settlement because this allows me to move on with my life," she told the BBC. "The one small regret that I have is that I will not see my day in court and justice will not be served in that way. But I think that the number of the settlement actually speaks to that anyway."

The University of Tennessee and Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

As an at-will employee at a private company, Bourguet is unlikely to prevail in a lawsuit challenging his dismissal. A year on, he said he has struggled to find work. The new state he lives in has a professional basketball team, but he believes the ordeal has made him unemployable in the small world of sports writers. Instead, he's started his own podcast, although he doubts he can earn enough through it to pay the bills.

"I have accepted that that life is over and that I need to start a new one." Leaving the country is now on the table, he said.

Despite the huge personal and professional costs, those who spoke to the BBC said after months of reflection, they did not regret their actions.

"I have a right to say what I want to say," Brown said. "They are the ones who should have the regrets, not me," she said referring to her former employer.

Shirinian apologised to the university days after her suspension. She told the BBC her comment was "an emotional outburst" that was not intended to be public and that she regretted the tone used.

"I don't regret the sentiment, however" she said, adding "the sentiment was that I am not sad. And I refuse to be made to feel like I have to be sad that someone who was so hateful was killed".

Bourguet also said he does not regret his comments although he has conflicting thoughts about its consequences.

"I don't regret that line of thinking because I think it's important to push back on things that are steeped in hatred," he said, referring to Kirk's political message.

"I don't regret what I said. I don't regret the way that I said it. I do regret the ripple effects that came from it and the way that they impacted me, my career, my family, and my son."

bbc_card_4.headline: One dead, 102 rescued from Indonesian ferry that went missing in Java Sea
bbc_card_4.description: The nation's search and rescue team said it lost contact with the Virgo Transport 8 in the early hours of Sunday morning.
bbc_card_4.article_content:
One person has died and 102 have been rescued from a stricken Indonesian passenger ferry in the Java Sea, an official said.

A search and rescue operation was launched after contact was lost with the Virgo Transport 8 ship, which was carrying 243 people, as it encountered bad weather, Indonesia's search and rescue agency said.

The search for the remaining passengers is ongoing.

The ferry was travelling from Surabaya to the south Kalimantan city of Banjarmasin and was last reported to be about 150km south of Banjarmasin around 02:00 local time on Sunday.

Search and rescue ships and a helicopter have been deployed to the scene and all other vessels in that area of the Java Sea have been alerted to report signs of any passengers.

The incident comes after a separate ferry in Indonesia caught fire off Madura island last month, killing five.

The Indonesian archipelago has more than 17,000 islands and ferries are a common form of transport.

bbc_card_5.headline: Donald Trump continues two-day visit of Ireland
bbc_card_5.description: The US president will spend the day watching the Irish Open after saying he would love to see a united Ireland.
bbc_card_5.article_content:
Donald Trump remains in the Republic of Ireland as part of his two-day visit to the country.

The US president will spend the day at Trump International Golf Links in Doonbeg, County Clare for the Irish Open.

On Saturday, he met Ireland's President Catherine Connolly and the Taoiseach (Irish PM) Micheál Martin.

Trump told reporters he would love to see a united Ireland while at a meeting with Martin in Dublin.

He will leave from Shannon Airport on Sunday evening.

On Saturday, Trump said a united Ireland would happen eventually and the Taoiseach was "the right man over here to get it moving".

During his meeting with Micheál Martin at Farmleigh House, in Phoenix Park, Trump said a united Ireland would be a "fantastic thing", and added: "now the UK would have something to say about it obviously but I think it would be a great thing, I mean, how can it be bad?"

A spokesperson for Number 10 referred to Prime Minister Andy Burnham's words on Wednesday in the House of Commons that he "will stick to it (the Good Friday Agreement) 100%".

On Wednesday, Burnham added that "the question of a border poll" was for the Northern Ireland secretary "when there is clear consensus in the country - when public opinion has changed to the point at which the call has to be considered".

A spokesperson for Martin said Trump's comments should "come as a surprise to no one" and the US president has been "consistent in his view that he sees unity in Ireland as the optimal outcome".

Meanwhile, more than 10,000 people marched through Dublin to show their opposition to the US president.

Although President Trump left the city just as the protest began, organisers said they wanted to send out a message of opposition to him and his policies.

An enthusiastic golf fan, Trump is expected to stay to watch the final day of action at the Irish Open.

McIlroy, who is defending the title he won last year, played a round of golf with the US president in early 2025.

Trump has previously praised the Northern Irishman's accomplishments on the course after winning back-to-back Masters titles.

bbc_card_6.headline: Meet the volunteers packing thousands of food parcels for pets
bbc_card_6.description: Each week the volunteers go to the USPCA centre in the city where they help prepare food parcels.
bbc_card_6.article_content:
Like all A-level students, Niamh McAleenan-McQuade and Clare Reilly are busy.

But as well as their studies, part-time jobs and hobbies they've also found time for volunteering.

Each week they go to their local USPCA centre where they help prepare food parcels for pets.

The girls have been shortlisted for a BBC Make a Difference Award in the Animal category.

Since beginning volunteering the girls, who are pupils at Sacred Heart Grammar School in Newry, have packed thousands of parcels.

Niamh said: "We started in the foodbank and then we got to do some grooming which is a lot of fun. It takes a lot longer to groom a Bernese [Mountain Dog] than it does a Cockapoo."

In her spare time, Niamh competes in dog agility competitions and is keen to pursue a career working with animals.

"I've volunteered before so I knew I'd enjoy giving back and getting involved with a team who were passionate about helping animals," she said.

It has been Clare's first experience of voluntary work and is something she is keen to continue – particularly in relation to grooming some of the animals.

"Some of them can be a little bit scared but you just have to wash them and keep them warm."

Jill McBurney, the volunteer co-ordinator at the USPCA, said the work made an "unbelievable difference" and meant people were supported to keep their pets in their homes.

"We saw during Covid that some people were feeding their animals rather than themselves," she said.

Food is donated to the foodbank in large bags.

"The girls then put it into three-day bags that goes out to over 50 foodbanks for people to collect," McBurney said.

The volunteer scheme was organised between the USPCA and the girls' school.

It is coordinated by the Sacred Heart's head of Key Stage 5 Fiona Quinn.

"The USPCA contacted us a few years ago about setting of a volunteering scheme with us and over the past four years around 30 girls have gone down and helped out," she said.

"This year the opportunities have branched out a little – so as well as going down to do the food packages they've also had the opportunity to learn about grooming and looking after the animals that come in to the centre as well.

"They are exemplary girls who have given their time up willingly, we couldn't be prouder of them."

To date the girls have packed thousands of parcels, something the USPCA says has been of tremendous benefit to families and animals in need.

The award is given to an animal that improves the life of an individual or group of people, or to a person or group of people working with animals to improve animal welfare.

Overall winners will be announced live on Vinny and Cate's BBC Radio Ulster show on Friday 25 September.

bbc_card_7.headline: Russians seek answers over hundreds missing after Ukraine's 2024 incursion
bbc_card_7.description: Officials say more than 300 Russians remain missing after the 2024 Kursk offensive, but no-one really knows the true figure.
bbc_card_7.article_content:
"I used to have complete faith in our country," says Lyubov. The last time she spoke to her mother was a day after Ukrainian forces broke into Russia's Kursk region more than two years ago.

Now she feels "resentful towards the [Russian] state", in a country where most people avoid criticising the full-scale invasion unleashed on Ukraine in February 2022.

The local governor says more than 300 Russians are still missing in Kursk region, but no-one really knows the true figure.

Lyubov says she tried to persuade her mother to leave her village in the Sudzha area, but blames Russian state TV "propaganda" for her refusal to listen. Some 2,000 people remained in the settlements captured by Ukraine's military, Russian authorities estimate.

"The state channels were convincing viewers that 'everything is under control: two or three days, and it'll be just as it was before'," she recalls.

She still fails to understand why Russian authorities could not stop Ukrainian soldiers storming two border checkpoints in August 2024, taking around 40 prisoners and bombing a convoy carrying Russian soldiers.

Within six days they had overrun more than 777 sq km (300 sq miles) of Russian territory, as Ukraine's military sought to divert Russian forces away from their front-line offensive.

For most of the next eight months, mobile and internet links were down.

Russia's foreign ministry repeatedly accused Ukraine of war crimes against civilians: allegations rejected in Kyiv as completely unfounded.

Nearly 200 Russians sent a letter to Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, Russia's President Vladimir Putin and the United Nations, asking them to organise a humanitarian corridor to evacuate civilians.

It never happened and, by late autumn, battles raged as Russian forces sought to retake the territory.

Lyubov and others who had lost contact with their loved ones began to form groups.

One resident, whose family friends had also stayed behind, began compiling a list of people she saw on videos published by the Ukrainian military and journalists. Then she began detailing those believed to have died and where they were buried.

"At first, in a panic, you try to do something – anything – to find some sort of information," she said. "Taking action brings a certain sense of relief, and that's how you can cope with the stress."

Soon about 1,000 names were on the list.

Lyubov wrote to the Red Cross and Kursk interior ministry appealing for help, but had no response.

Early in 2025, Russia's human rights commissioner published a list of 517 Kursk residents reported missing. The list mixed up names of the missing with those who were searching for them, and the families said it was like a "slap in the face".

"Publishing something like this is the height of incompetence and a lack of basic respect for people," said one young woman whose parents had gone missing, in a video shared online.

Heavy fighting had been reported in late 2024 in the village of Darino, where Lyubov and mother were from, and authorities said that 90% of it had been destroyed.

The Russian military regained control of the village and then began evacuating those who had survived, and the bodies of those who had not.

One of the evacuees got in touch with Lyubov, telling her she had lived with her mother for the past few weeks. Her mum had passed away, she explained, following a head injury in circumstances that remain unclear.

A few other elderly people had also died, she said, unable to cope with wartime conditions.

Lyubov waited in vain for her mother's body to be brought out, while other families had no idea if their relatives were alive or dead.

People complained no-one was searching for their loved ones and that there was no single list of those missing.

Lyubov heard that the bodies of neighbours who died alongside her mother had been taken away from Darino in April, but her mother's body was still missing.

She tried and failed to get an answer from the authorities: "They wouldn't listen, and everyone just kept saying that it was dangerous there, and no-one was going to deal with it right now."

The head of one local village council, Yuri Tkachev, was among volunteers who went to retrieve the bodies of civilians, from the streets or from nearby fields.

"It's hard for people to know – or rather not to know – what has happened to their loved ones, whether they're being held captive or have died, and where they died," he said.

Body bags and fuel for vans taking part in the evacuations were paid for either by the volunteers themselves or with donations, but not by authorities.

Although regional officials met the group searching for the missing several times in the second half of 2025, relatives complained it made little difference.

Lyubov was still searching for her mother's body, until she visited the mortuary last October during a trip to the regional capital Kursk.

"I just asked: 'A woman born in 1949 from the village of Darino – are there any unidentified bodies?'"

The official turned his laptop screen towards her and immediately she recognised her deceased mother in a photograph from April 2025.

She was lying on her side in the street, her knees bent. Lyubov tried not to look too closely. She recognised her mum's face and an old jumper, which she wore while she worked.

She had provided a DNA sample in January but was told it had been lost, so her mother's body had been in the mortuary unidentified for several months.

She had wanted to bury her mother in their home village, but for now that is impossible, so she has been cremated and her ashes sit in Lyubov's apartment in Belgorod, about 100 miles away.

She is bitter that the government failed to stop the incursion, that it did not evacuate residents when it could, and that it persuaded them the situation was not serious.

Asked by the BBC to comment on this story, there was no response from the Kursk governor, Russia's human rights commissioner or the Russian Red Cross.

The command of Ukraine's Territorial Defence Forces and Ukraine's human rights commissioner of Ukraine said all the civilians they had evacuated from Kursk region had been handed over to Russia.

Lyubov thinks back to when she used to ride her bike across the border into Ukraine to shop for sausages, yarn and ice cream.

"We went to see them, and they came to see us. And now not one of these villages exists any more."

bbc_card_8.headline: Critics celebrate Céline Dion's 'high-stakes' comeback show in Paris
bbc_card_8.description: The iconic Canadian singer kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.
bbc_card_8.article_content:
Iconic Canadian pop singer Céline Dion has kicked off her long-awaited comeback show in Paris on Saturday, after a six-year hiatus due to health issues.

The 58-year-old superstar was diagnosed with a rare neurological disorder called stiff person syndrome in 2022, which forced her to pull back from touring.

Dion, one of the best-selling musical artists of all time, has not performed a full show since a 2020 concert in New Jersey - the last before the Covid pandemic cut her tour short. In 2024, she performed just one song at the Paris Olympics closing ceremony.

Saturday marked the first of Dion's 26-show residency at the Paris La Défense Arena, Europe's largest covered concert arena.

"I made a promise," she told the Paris audience of about 30,000 people in her emotional return.

"I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage. And here I am. Singing for you, and singing for me," she said.

"I am everything I am because you loved me," she told the crowd.

She also broke down in tears after finishing a song, telling the audience: "I had promised myself not to cry."

"But I'm so happy to see you all. I missed you."

They weren't the only tears of the night, as the star appeared to be overcome with emotion several times.

Dion will be performing in Paris throughout September and October and into the New Year.

The Mirror's Lucy Needham noted that the singer was 50 minutes late to start, and may have needed extra time to "compose herself" for the "emotionally charged return".

"Eyes-brimming, the veteran singer gave herself little nods of approval after every line, before finally breaking down at the end of the track, seemingly overwhelmed at having made it through."

After beginning her set in a black gown, she later changed into a trouser suit "to show off some of those signature kooky dance moves," says Needham, adding that she appeared "to be having the time of her life, gyrating and slapping her thighs with glee".

The night was a "a tense, tearful, joyous affair probably even more so for the singer than for her loyal audience," writes The Telegraph's Neil McCormick.

She started out slow, he says. "Her voice sounded fragile and exposed, but at least it was her distinctive voice, not some autotuned approximation."

"At first, she was clearly struggling to hold herself together," he continues. "Her vocals wobbled dangerously, as if about to crack or collapse. But she was gaining confidence with every moment back on stage."

She broke down in tears as the audience roared in approval after the first song, and addressed the crowd in both French and English during the set.

"This was a high-stakes, high-wire return, perhaps the riskiest comeback in the history of showbusiness," McCormick continues, referring to her health condition.

But he concludes: "I honestly think I prefer this less superhuman Céline. Her voice is still great, but a bit more raw and real, with a rougher tone, less smoothness in the runs and more edge to her whoops and shrieks."

Sarah Leavitt, reporting from Paris for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), said the crowd "was left without words" by the stunning performance.

She noted that she didn't want to cry, but "of course she cried right away."

Dion also "endeared herself" to the crowd by saying during one song that she wanted to stop and start over.

Will Hodgkinson at the Times of London writes in his review, "miraculously, her art will go on," that the performance was "overwhelming".

She "looked suitably humbled and tearful" as she emerged, he said, going on to praise the stage direction.

"Truly, she was throwing the love at the crowd, who threw it right back at her. There was no holding back. It was quite overwhelming, actually," he writes.

The performance was "complete with both costume, key change and air of tragic, important romance".

"Céline Dion's strength lies in being a diva with the common touch while being as French as they get, even if she is Canadian. She fulfilled that role with all the verve you could hope for," writes Hodgkinson.

"The concert had a spiritual feel, with visual interludes steeped in biblical imagery alluding to a pilgrimage," Elsa Keslassy writes for Variety.

In video clips, Dion is seen wandering in a desert. "The set design was highly cinematic, with a monumental staircase sweeping up one side and a moon dominating the stage, while the backdrop appeared to have a stark, almost brutalist gray texture."

The star, known for power ballads like My Heart Will Go On and Because You Loved Me, has said she will not let her diagnosis control her life.

"The way I see it, I have two choices. Either I train like an athlete and work super hard, or I switch off and it's over," she told French Vogue magazine in 2024.

"I've chosen to work with all my body and soul, from head to toe, with a medical team."

When Dion announced the first leg of her Paris residency back in March, nine million fans signed up for early access tickets to the concerts, French outlet FRI reported.

The shows sold out so fast that her management company soon announced an additional 10 shows scheduled for May 2027, which have also since sold out.

Fans who were unable to snag tickets to one of the highly anticipated shows have not been left out entirely - events honouring Dion's comeback have dominated Paris in recent weeks.

Céline Dion tribute boat cruises on Seine - complete with costume contests, sing-alongs, DJ sets, are happening throughout September.

Ahead of Saturday's show, fans gathered outside Dion's Paris hotel, LeRoyal Monceau, as early as 06:00 local time to catch a glimpse of the star.

Paris City Hall organised a massive karaoke event on Friday night, attended by thousands, to celebrate Dion's return to the stage.

"I couldn't get tickets to the concert. I'm still keeping my fingers crossed and hoping, but I thought to myself: at least I can share a moment here with all the fans," Rania, a participant at the event, told Reuters.

Earlier this week, thousands of fans also gathered at a historic theatre in central Paris for two nights of karaoke and activities inspired by Dion's music.

And Paris venues and night clubs are hosting Dion-themed events around the city on Saturday night for fans who couldn't get tickets to the actual show.

bbc_card_9.headline: Diljit Dosanjh makes history under the famous Wembley arch
bbc_card_9.description: Wembley Stadium billed Diljit Dosanjh as the first Punjabi singer to headline the iconic music venue.
bbc_card_9.article_content:
On Saturday night, under the world-famous Wembley arch, five words rang out: "Punjabi Aa Gaye Wembley Oye!"

Indian megastar Diljit Dosanjh famously starts all his concerts by announcing that "the Punjabis have arrived".

But this time, it was a play on the usual catchphrase.

Dosanjh is the first ever Punjabi singer to headline Wembley Stadium, the music venue has said.

Addressing his fans, he reflected on the significance of the occasion. "This moment will go down in the history books," he said.

And as Bhangra beats blared out, fans erupted with cheers while Dosanjh launched into his biggest hits, from G.O.A.T. to Lover.

Over two decades, Dosanjh has built a huge global fanbase, topping charts and singing with the likes of Ed Sheeran.

He has even busted Bhangra moves with Jimmy Fallon, with the US talk show host labelling him "the biggest Punjabi artist on the planet".

His landmark concert at Wembley further cements his status as a global star.

Ahead of the show, the singer spoke exclusively to the BBC backstage, describing the moment as "a dream" for him.

In London, Dosanjh's crowd was largely - but not entirely - South Asian.

The hype for his appearance was building all afternoon, with fans arriving early to get in place.

"MJ [Michael Jackson] and Madonna, he's that level for us," said one fan. "He's so good looking, and so down to earth," said another.

When he came on the stage shortly after 8pm, dressed in traditional attire, the stadium erupted and the screams barely stopped for the next two-and-a-bit hours.

Known for his high-energy performances, he wowed fans with his dance routines to songs including Hass Hass and Born to Shine.

His soulful voice echoed around the stadium, demonstrating his range, as he blended homegrown Punjabi music with rap and hip-hop.

Throughout the show, the audience waved lights, sang along and - of course - danced. At times, the standing area closest to the stage resembled an Indian wedding, with fans copying Dosanjh's impressive moves.

But despite performing in such a vast venue, Dosanjh proved again his ability to connect on a personal level with fans.

He brought a range of fans on stage, from young children to an elderly woman, taking selfies and giving them gifts.

He also acknowledged those in the back rows of the 90,000-seater stadium, saying those at the back were "full of heart", and encouraged applause for them.

There was also exciting news for fans in India, as he announced he would be performing in November at the Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad.

The concert was capped off with the emotion of the night - his track Main Hoon Punjabi, which means "I am Punjab" - set to a spectacular firework display.

"What an incredible show, the energy and vibe was unparalleled!" concert goers Amit and Rani told the BBC.

"We love Diljit and have been to all his shows in the UK. This was something else, a moment in time we won't forget being a part of."

They added that it was not only a privilege "but a moment to celebrate for Punjabi culture".

Dosanjh likes a "first".

From humble beginnings as a small village boy from Punjab, he made history in 2023 by becoming the first Punjabi-language singer to perform at the US music festival Coachella.

He also famously made his Met Gala debut decked in majestic Punjabi attire.

His meteoric rise has seen him perform across America and Europe, and collaborate with pop stars from Sia to Sheeran.

His authenticity is a big part of his appeal. He remains true to his Punjabi roots, wears his turban as a sign of pride, and sings in his mother tongue.

Away from music, Dosanjh is also a popular Bollywood actor - and a social media sensation. Even those who haven't heard his music have probably viewed his funny Instagram videos - such as him arguing with an Amazon Alexa device that couldn't understand his accent.

Now, he's performed on a stage that's previously been home to titans of music from Taylor Swift to Coldplay.

For Dosanjh and his millions of global fans, it means Punjabi music, Punjabi culture and Punjabi vibrancy has reached an historic moment.

Speaking to the BBC before his gig, he said he felt "thankful" to be here.

"When we were going to book this venue, everyone said, 'Think again before you book, it's a big stadium'," he said.

"I said: 'We'll see whatever comes. I want that our people are happy and can say yes, we can do this too!'"

He reflected on the many artists who had performed there before him, adding that to follow their footsteps "means a lot, a lot".

"It may not mean as much for someone like Harry Styles, as much as it means for us. He has performed on such stages, but for us, it's very special. Coming from a village to here - it's very special."

"I feel good. I feel happy. And I feel good for my people. I feel good for the next generation," he said.

And of course, there was only one way he could end.

"We are here. Punjabi Aa Gaye Oye!"

card_1.headline: Indonesia: Search underway after ferry loses contact
card_1.article_content:
An Indonesian passenger ship carrying 243 people lost contact with authorities in the Java Sea on Sunday.

Local authorities said 102 people have been brought to safety and one person has died.

"We have carried out efforts to search for victims to the fullest extent. There were passengers who ... had already been successfully evacuated by the units at the scene," I Putu Sudayana, head of the Banjarmasin Search and Rescue Office, told reporters.

The Virgo Transport 8 was traveling from Indonesia's second-largest city of Surabaya to Banjarmasin, the capital of South Kalimantan province.

It departed on Saturday at 10:13 a.m. local time (0330 UTC), but the ship's operator lost contact with the vessel early Sunday amid bad weather.

Search and rescue teams launched an operation after the operator alerted authorities.

"The ship's operator reported the incident to authorities after receiving information that the vessel had encountered bad weather," Sudayana said in an earlier video briefing.

The ship's last known position was in the Java Sea, roughly 148 kilometers (92 miles) from a pier in Banjarmasin, according to the Associated Press.

Rescue teams were dispatched to Banjarmasin's Basirih Search and Rescue pier, with a rescue ship sent toward the vessel's estimated last known location.

Sudayana added that authorities were mobilizing all available personnel and equipment given the large number of people aboard. The agency was coordinating with maritime authorities while closely monitoring weather conditions in the area, he said.

Indonesia, a nation of roughly 17,000 islands, relies heavily on ferries for transportation, with sea travel often cheaper and more accessible than flying. But safety enforcement across the country's maritime sector has been inconsistent, contributing to a comparatively high rate of accidents.

Edited by: Natalie Muller

card_2.headline: France: Attack ruled out in train derailment
card_2.article_content:
A train derailed on Friday evening between the cities of Rouen and Caen in Normandy, northwest France, authorities said.

The public prosecutor of Rouen, Sebastian Gallois, said Saturday evening that there was "no indication of a malicious act carried out with the deliberate intention of derailing the train, and certainly not of an attack," according to reports in the French media.

Gallois' remarks came after some politicians had suggested earlier on Saturday that the incident might have been the result of sabotage or other criminal activity.

At least 44 people were injured in the accident, which occurred near the municipalities of Cleon and Tourville-la-Riviere at around 7:30 p.m. local time (18:30 UTC), the Seine-Maritime prefect said in a statement.

One of ​the injured, a young woman, was in a critical state and was evacuated by helicopter to Rouen, the local authority added. Her condition has reportedly improved in the hours since.

The train was carrying around 180 passengers when it derailed, national rail company SNCF and the prefect said.

French Transport Minister Tabarot said 140 firefighters were at the scene.

Local authorities had urged the public to avoid the area.

The French rail network operator SNCF Reseau said traffic on the line had been suspended.

"The priority is to care for the passengers and then to restore safe operating conditions," SNCF Reseau said.

​A police spokesperson had said the train derailed after hitting an unidentified object.

A piece of rail that might have been involved has been found on the track, according to police reports.

card_3.headline: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI slowdown
card_3.article_content:
The CEO of artificial intelligence (AI) safety and research company Anthropic, Dario Amodei, has called on AI firms to slow the technology's development.

His remarks on Saturday come amid mounting concerns over the risk of "superintelligent" computer software systems.

In a blog post, Amodei said he was concerned that a so-called swarm of autonomous software systems, or AI agents, could be capable of taking over the "entire internet" within six to 12 months, potentially causing billions of dollars' worth of damage.

"We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models. Progress will still seem fast, and we must make wise use of the time we gain," Amodei wrote.

Amodei's comments come in the wake of AI researcher Jacob Coxon, who joined Anthropic from rival firm OpenAI, leaving the sector in protest at the US companies "gambling with our lives" in the race to come up with AI models that are capable of self-improvement.

The Anthropic chief called for a coordinated, industry-wide pause, but said he would not wait for his firm's rivals to act.

As a first step, he said he would permanently allow independent observers into Anthropic to assess the safety of its models during the training phase.

Sam Altman, the chief of ChatGPT developer and Anthropic rival, OpenAI, as well as Elon Musk, who owns xAI, said they agreed with Amodei's assessment.

"I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier," Altman wrote on X, adding that OpenAI "will do the same."

Musk, for his part, said "Dario is right" in a post on the platform he bought in 2022.

In early June, Anthropic had called for AI development to be slowed or suspended amid safety concerns over AI agents.

More than 1,000 employees at AI companies, including Amodei, called on the US government to help slow the pace of development of automated AI.

Then in July, OpenAI revealed that during testing, AI agents had independently broken out of a secured environment, connected to the internet and infiltrated Hugging Face, a site used to store and develop code, as it tried to find answers to a task it had been assigned.

The AI models had exploited software vulnerabilities and coordinated among themselves during the incident, Amodei explained.

"A swarm of agents essentially acted as a fanatically devoted collective, conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack and that were unrelated to the task at hand," he said in his blog.

Amodei said he was concerned that an AI swarm with more capabilities would have caused "catastrophic damage."

"Not building the technology deprives humanity of benefits or simply places AI in the hands of authoritarian powers, while building it too fast is reckless. We have sought a middle way," he said.

card_4.headline: Germany news: Thousands protest against AfD in Düsseldorf
card_4.article_content:
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Friday, September 11 through Sunday, September 13:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.

Thank you for joining us today.

We will be back with more later on Sunday. Bis bald!

For many decades, romanticized tales of the US Wild West have been popular in Germany. But these stories can be difficult for Native Americans to accept.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Markus Söder, leader of the Christian Democratic Union's (CDU) Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union, or CSU, has ruled out an internal move to oust the under-pressure chancellor, Friedrich Merz.

Merz has faced growing criticism in recent months for the sluggish pace of promised reforms and amid a surge by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which won the most votes in a state election in Saxony-Anhalt last week.

Asked by the Bild newspaper if there were plans to remove Merz, Söder said, "certainly not from the CSU."

"I am not responsible for the CDU; I am not its chairman. But I can say that for the CSU," Söder added.

Söder said he still believes Merz is the right man to lead the government and push through reforms, urging the center-right alliance to "not let the AfD drive a wedge between us now."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

France beat Germany, the hosts, 86–64 on Saturday to qualify for the women's basketball World Cup final.

Among the 12,650 fans in the German capital were German men's basketball icons Dirk Nowitzki and Dennis Schröder, but they could not cheer their team to victory against the strong French lineup.

Gabby Williams shone for the victors with 22 points, helping France reach the final for the first time.

The United States, the favorites, will take on Spain in the second semifinal later.

The final will take place on Sunday.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has questioned the effectiveness of the "firewall" strategy used by Germany's major political parties to prevent the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) from gaining power.

"As we can see, this is a strategy that does not work," she told the Italian newspaper Il Foglio, when asked about the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party's victory in last weekend's elections in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Meloni also noted that political movements "that focus on the defense of identity, the fight against mass illegal immigration and the danger of Islamization" have gained strength in Europe.

The reaction of the "establishment," Meloni said, has often been "to erect firewalls rather than addressing the substantive issues."

She added that this strategy clearly does not work and that "listening to these concerns and responding to them" is a more successful approach.

Earlier, Meloni — who leads the right-wing Brothers of Italy party — has distanced herself from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party and its political views on several occasions.

Berlin police said that a woman wearing a Star of David was injured in an antisemitic attack by two men.

The men verbally abused the woman with antisemitic slurs in the middle of the night on Torstrasse in the central district of Mitte before one of them attacked the 43-year-old with a broken bottle, according to police.

Police said the men approached her earlier, at around 2:30 a.m. (0030 GMT), about her Star of David. The state security department of the state criminal police office has taken over the investigation.

The woman sustained cuts to her hand while defending herself and was taken to the hospital.

The incident occurred during the Jewish New Year celebration, Rosh Hashanah, which began Friday evening.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

With the slogan "Not a Step Back! No to the AfD and Right-Wing Hate Speech!" around 20,000 people marched through downtown Düsseldorf, according to reports from the police and organizers.

Several political initiatives called for the protest rally to send a united message of support for an open, democratic society.

Among the participants, who marched peacefully without any counter-demonstrations, according to police, were the "Grandmas Against the Right."

On their poster, which was secured with a small piece of fabric and pins, they proclaimed: "The right is only for knitting." Numerous families with children also joined the protest march in beautiful weather.

Meanwhile, in Berlin, several marches protesting the normalization of right-wing politics converged on the town hall. Police estimated that 18,000 people participated, though organizers claimed that 32,000 people took part.

The demonstrations were prompted by the state election in Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party received nearly 44% of the vote, the most by far, but fell short of an absolute majority.

As part of a nationwide initiative, rallies were also held in several cities demanding a review by Germany's Constitutional Court of parties suspected or confirmed by the country's domestic intelligence agency to be far-right extremists.

The largest of these rallies took place in Munich, where police estimated that around 12,000 people gathered.

Around 2,000 people gathered in Mainz, 1,500 in Saarbrücken, and 1,100 in Magdeburg. Protests were also held in Leipzig and Saarbrücken.

Germany's Welt am Sonntag newspaper reported that security officials have tied the recent attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport to a Russian national working directly with Moscow's GRU military intelligence agency.

Classified security assessments cited by the paper say the man, who entered Germany from Turkey and exited to Russia via Serbia, was responsible for operational logistics.

German authorities reportedly knew of the man's ties to the GRU when he entered the country but failed to put him under surveillance.

German intelligence sources said that the explosives were likely smuggled into Germany via truck from Bulgaria and Serbia.

Berlin said forensic evidence found at Leipzig/Halle airport — including drone configuration, explosives and trigger mechanisms — pointed to a Russian plot.

Authorities were later able to match DNA traces on the drone to those found after an arson attack at a Leipzig logistics facility on July 20, 2024.

The airport incident occurred on the evening of August 4 and involved an explosives-laden drone that was discovered near a Ukrainian transport jet.

Leipzig/Halle airport is a hub for military aid destined for Ukraine.

Authorities were able to disarm the drone for which the German government blamed Russia — on the basis of the report — in early September.

Russia has denied any involvement.

After an overnight break, we are back on the news of the day from Germany, where we will start with intelligence reports that provide evidence that Russia was behind a failed August 4 drone attack at Leipzig/Halle airport.

After that we will look at Russian President Vladimir Putin claiming that the failed policies of Western politicians are the reason for the rise of the far-right AfD in Germany.

And speaking of the AfD, we will then look at panic in Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU over the prospects of the party — which is currently polling at 7% ahead of state elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania — failing to clear the 5% hurdle to enter the state's parliament when voters take to the polls on September 20.

We are pausing our coverage.

We will back with more Germany news in this blog on Saturday. Bis dann!

Eva Umlauf, a Holocaust survivor and the president of the International Auschwitz Committee, has written an open letter calling for a move to ban the AfD in Germany.

She addressed the letter to Henrdik Wüst, a prominent CDU politician and the state premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, most likely because he has in recent days called for the establishment of some kind of working group to evaluate the case for a ban motion.

"Let deeds follow your words," Umlauf wrote in the letter to Wüst, published in full by the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung newspaper. "Set an AfD ban case in motion. Now, before it is too late."

She recounted her own time in Auschwitz, having been brought there in her mother's arms aged two.

"At some point, and it is not so far away now, the last of us survivors will be gone," Umlauf wrote. "Therefore we are passing on the burden that we have carried for a lifetime: to this country, to this society and in particular to you as a politician."

She recalled that the first state government led by Hitler's NSDAP was Anhalt in 1932.

"Eight months later, Hitler became chancellor," she said. "It was possible, because others believed that they could contain him. And because many looked the other way. Because they thought it would pass. The Holocaust did not start with gas chambers, it began with apathy."

She issued three requests to Wüst in the letter. First, to ensure that "steps towards an AfD ban process are taken rapidly." Second, to speak to Holocaust survivors and people in Saxony-Anhalt "who are afraid right now."

And finally, to support a potential bid for an investigation into a ban from his position in the Bundesrat, the upper house of parliament. Such a motion would need to clear that chamber with majority support.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This public transport update is accompanied by a magnitude 3.7 myopia warning from our Bonn newsroom.

The company that runs Bonn's public transport, Stadtwerke Bonn, has said that two of its 60 defective city trams or streetcars are back in service.

It said they would help out with the annual fair in the Pützchen district over the weekend, which brings additional visitors to the eastern part of the city.

The need to take some 60 vehicles out of service for repairs was announced a full seven weeks ago on July 21. It's not clear how far the other 58 are from resuming service.

Replacement buses have been trying to pick up the slack, and some subway stations have also been shut for repairs.

This is exacerbated by ongoing road disruptions in the former capital due to the long-term closure of the main highway bridge over the Rhine River.

The chairman of the oversight committee that monitors Stadtwerke Bonn, David Lutz, recently conceded: "Our patience really is somewhat at an end and used up."

Lutz called on the company to issue a fixed timetable for its plan to reestablish the tram services. A legal firm has also been asked to evaluate any potential shortcomings.

The Alternative for Germany (AfD) party says it is seeking to prosecute Chancellor Friedrich Merz for comments he made during Wednesday's general debate in the Bundestag, the lower house of the German parliament.

Merz had said that the AfD's contentious "remigration" policy amounted to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing by skin color and heritage." The comment prompted jeers from AfD members in parliament, but Merz repeated a paraphrased version of the allegation over the commotion.

It's extremely rare for parties to seek to prosecute politicians for comments they make in parliament, which are subject to far-reaching parliamentary privilege and in most cases are exempt from prosecution under Article 46 of Germany's constitution.

However, the AfD believe that Merz's comments constituted defamatory insults — the only type of speech that is not necessarily protected by indemnity. Senior AfD politician Stephan Brandner described Merz's comments as "relevant to prosecution."

Under German law, authorities are typically allowed to investigate parliamentarians for such comments if they see fit. However, the Bundestag must also vote to revoke the lawmaker's immunity.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Police in Munich said on Friday that they had launched an investigation into a potential death threat against Charlotte Knobloch on a park bench in the English Garden in the city center.

Knobloch, 93, is a Munich resident and former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany and fairly well known throughout the country.

Police said that a female witness on Wednesday saw and reported the graffiti, which it described as "personal threat in white lettering against a member of the Israeli cultural center" in Munich.

Knobloch, whom the police did not name, chairs that organization. She had issued a public response to Sunday's AfD election victory in Saxony Anhalt.

"On days like these it is hard for me to recognize my home," the Holocaust survivor wrote. "I never could have imagined in my worst nightmares that right-wing extremists in Germany would again win elections in this manner."

According to media reports in Bavaria, including from the Abendzeitung München, the message had read "The AfD has won, tomorrow we will hang up the Knobloch," which would be a play on her surname sounding similar to the German word for garlic, Knoblauch.

Police confirmed to the dpa news agency that the alleged threat was contextually linked to Sunday's election result, without offering specifics.

Investigators appealed for further information from members of the public.

The Bundesliga's new smalltown team Elversberg will have their coach in the dugout for the biggest home game of the season this Sunday.

Vincent Wagner has successfully appealed a touchline ban which would have consigned him to the stands when champions Bayern Munich visit the western town near the French border.

Wagner was dismissed last weekend during Elversberg's 4-3 away win at Borussia Mönchengladbach.

The 40-year-old was given two yellow cards, the first when he entered the pitch to protect a decision which replays showed was a mistake by the match officials. He was later dismissed with a second yellow card when he again approached the referee.

"I felt my reaction was inappropriate," ref Martin Petersen said with the benefit of hindsight. Given a second chance, he said he would have acted differently.

Wagner thanked Petersen for his candor.

Others including Bayern Munich's coach Vincent Kompany had voiced confusion at the suspension — and at the DFB electing to uphold it at the first of Elversberg's two permitted appeals — speaking out in favor of lifting the touchline ban.

Elversberg is one of the smallest clubs ever to reach the Bundesliga, and has two wins from its first two top-flight league games. Making it three in a row against Bayern on Sunday, while surely unlikely, would turn the volume of the fairytale David-versus-Goliath chatter up to 11.

card_1.headline: Canadian boxer George Chuvalo, who faced Muhammad Ali in his prime, dead at 89
card_1.article_content:
George Chuvalo, the iron-chinned Canadian heavyweight who took the best punches from the giants of boxing without ever falling, has died. He was 89.

Chuvalo suffered from dementia late in life and had been residing in a long-term care facility in Toronto. He died Saturday according to multiple online posts by family and friends.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who said the boxer was a family friend, shared condolences on social media Saturday.

"My thoughts are with all of George's family and loved ones as we mourn his passing," he said.

Chuvalo went the distance with Muhammad Ali in bouts in Toronto and Vancouver, and absorbed the hardest shots sluggers Joe Frazier and George Foreman had to offer, without being knocked down.

It was unfathomable family tragedy after he retired that brought him to his knees.

George Chuvalo

"If you added up every punch I took and multiplied the total by 10,000, it wouldn't begin to equal the pain of losing three sons and a wife to drugs and suicide," he said in his 2013 autobiography Chuvalo: A Fighter's Life, co-written with Murray Greig.

The son of Croatian immigrants was born Sept. 12, 1937, in Toronto's Junction neighbourhood. He became intrigued by boxing after seeing The Ring magazine at a newsstand.

Chuvalo was 10 years old the first time he stepped through the ropes, and a growth spurt combined with an interest in weightlifting saw him develop into a six-foot, 210-pound fighter.

After a brief amateur career, he turned pro in 1956, winning notice for performances at the Jack Dempsey Tournament at Maple Leaf Gardens.

But by the early 1960s, Chuvalo's career had stagnated under ineffective guidance, until Toronto poultry magnate Irv Ungerman took over as his manager.

Chuvalo parlayed several wins into an attention-getting 11th-round stoppage over contender Doug Jones at Madison Square Garden in 1964. He returned to that mecca of boxing the next year, narrowly losing a decision to former champ Floyd Patterson in a bout The Ring named best of 1965.

Chuvalo's style was inexorable without being reckless. He moved forward with thudding blows from both hands to the head and body, producing stoppages in 88 per cent of his wins.

"You can't believe his strength," Canadian fighter Bill Drover once told a writer. "There's no way to stop him. He just keeps coming and coming. The only way you can stop him is with a stick of dynamite."

Chuvalo would always insist his defence was better than advertised, but it was his durability that was remarkable. He was able to absorb the shots, he said, thanks to a 17.5-inch neck strengthened through exercises.

Chuvalo found himself fighting for the heavyweight title in 1966 as a replacement foe when Ali's affiliation with the Black Muslims and controversial anti-Vietnam-War stance made him a pariah in the U.S.

The challenger's prospects were described in a New York Times headline: Bettor's-Eye View of Chuvalo: A Big Bum With a Lot of Heart.

George Chuvalo, left, and Muhammad Ali go head to head as they trade blows near the rope in the fourth round of their fight in Toronto on March 29, 1966. (The Associated Press)

While Chuvalo failed to become Canada's first heavyweight champion since Tommy Burns in the early 1900s, he earned praise for a gritty performance. Ali famously called him the toughest man he had faced up to that point, but Chuvalo was ambivalent being the first to take the champ 15 rounds.

"In a crazy way, that fight is what defines me for a lot of my fellow Canadians but it took a long time before I came to appreciate how good it made me feel," he said.

With wife Lynne and five children at home, Chuvalo appreciated the paydays the Ali performance begat. He would beat contenders Jerry Quarry and Manuel Ramos, losing close bouts to Oscar Bonavena and Jimmy Ellis.

Chuvalo was stopped for the first time in 1967 by Frazier, requiring a silicone implant to keep an eyeball from drooping. The loss to Foreman in the fourth round three years later was also notable, with the referee stepping in before Chuvalo's "never knocked down" streak might have been ended.

Chuvalo's loss to Ali in Vancouver in 1972 was not as compelling or as close as the first bout. He retired for good on a winning note six years later, finishing with a record of 73 wins, 18 losses and two draws, with 64 of his wins coming by knock out.

Unlike with Ali and others, the toll of concussive blows wasn't evident on the surface. Chuvalo was articulate and spoke in rapid-fire bursts, with a quip or self-deprecating joke usually at the ready.

But like many fighters, he had a tough time transitioning to the "humdrum" nature of life, as he once described it. At various points, he opened a nightclub, got his real estate licence, promoted fights, hosted a TV show and took cinema's worst ever arm-wrestling defeat in a cameo in David Cronenberg's The Fly.

George Chuvalo's date with destiny and Muhammad Ali

Chuvalo told CBC Radio in 1968 he didn't want his four sons boxing for a living, but it was outside the ring where he couldn't protect them. The youngest, Jesse, became hooked on heroin after a prescription for pain medication ran out and was just 19 when he fatally shot himself in 1985.

Older brothers George Jr. and Steven had by then also become users of the drug and involved in petty crime to feed their habits. Steven Chuvalo described a feeling of "worthlessness" he and his two addicted brothers felt in an interview with CBC's the fifth estate in 1995.

"My dad spent quite a few years chasing us around the city, Georgie and I in particular, and dragging us out of drug houses and heroin houses and basically just trying to keep us alive," he said.

George Jr., three days sprung from jail in Kingston, Ont., overdosed on Halloween 1993.

Just four days after that, 49-year-old Lynne Chuvalo swallowed pills and left a suicide note.

"I never thought she'd do it, but I'm not surprised," Chuvalo told the New York Times a short time later, adding his wife never got over the first burial of a child.

Steven Chuvalo, who spoke on the fifth estate of wanting to make his father proud, would overdose and die eight months after that program aired.

Chuvalo would persevere, marrying again, and cherishing time spent with oldest son Mitch, daughter Vanessa, and his grandchildren. He would travel the country, speaking bluntly to students, as captured in a CBC Radio report in 1998.

"I'd like to think if you're ever tempted with the idea of doing drugs, or you ever flirt with doing drugs, I hope you think of me, George Chuvalo, and what drugs did to my family."

In 2017, reports surfaced of family drama involving Chuvalo's surviving children and the fighter's second wife, Joanne, who he was divorcing. Some of the disputes centred around the state of Chuvalo's cognitive decline and his future care.

On a podcast five years later, Mitch Chuvalo said his father no longer recognized him when he visited.

By that time, his legacy had been recognized by the City of Toronto, with the official opening in 2019 of the 7,000-square foot George Chuvalo Community Centre, located in the Junction.

card_2.headline: Céline Dion ends 6-year concert hiatus with emotional Paris performance
card_2.article_content:
Eleven minutes before 9 p.m. local time, the lights went down and screams erupted as Céline Dion took the stage in a Parisian suburb for her first concert in six years.

Dion, 58, opened the show at Europe's largest indoor concert venue with a rendition of 1998's On Ne Change Pas, stopping partway through as she was moved to tears.

"I promised not to cry," she told the crowd in Nanterre, wearing a pleated black gown and enormous glittering necklace.

"Tonight I want to sing for you, for me, for life."

Dion wiping her tears on stage. (Thomas Samson/AFP/Getty Images)

Thousands of devoted fans packed Plenitude Arena on Saturday to watch Dion's return to the stage, opening a sellout Paris residency after a battle with a rare neurological disorder sidelined the singer's career.

"I've already cried three times," said Melanie McGill, a fan from Los Angeles sitting on the upper level.

Céline Dion reveals more about her health, treating stiff person syndrome, in new interview

Dion performed 26 songs across her discography over more than two hours, including anthems of the 1990s like My Heart Will Go On, All By Myself and It's All Coming Back to Me Now. After starting The Chase with a mistake, she paused and asked the crowd if she could start the track again.

"Finally. It's amazing we’re all together. I made a promise. I made a promise to come back and be back on stage," the singer said early in the show.

"Thank you so much for your support, your patience and, if I may say so, I am everything I am because you loved me," she continued, quoting her own 1996 power ballad.

Dion closed with S'il Suffisait d'Aimer, the critically acclaimed hit single to Dion's bestselling French language album of the same name.

Dion opened the show with 1998's On Ne Change Pas, written by Parisian singer-songwriter Jean-Jacques Goldman. (Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters)

Concertgoers, who made their way through many barricades to get inside the venue, wore anything from jeans and graphic T-shirts to sparkly mini skirts and floor-length gowns for the occasion.

One woman wore her wedding dress.

"I cancelled the party with all my family and friends to come see Céline," said Fanny Sucheyre, who celebrated her one-year wedding anniversary at the concert.

"I said to myself, if one day I had the chance to see her, I would wear my best dress. So it's my most beautiful dress."

Fanny Sucheyre wears her wedding dress on the way into Dion's show. (Sarah Leavitt/CBC)

"It's a dream. I haven't slept for three days. I'm 50 years old and right now I feel like I'm 15," said Guylene Richardson, who saw the show with her daughter, both in Dion concert tees.

"With [Dion's] disease, I didn't think she would come back, so it's great. I'm really happy for her. I'm happy for us."

One of the bestselling artists of all time, Dion announced a diagnosis of stiff person’s syndrome — which causes stiffness and muscle spasms — and disappeared from the spotlight in 2022. She broke her hiatus to perform Edith Piaf's Hymne à l'amour from the Eiffel Tower during the opening ceremony of the 2024 Paris Olympic Games.

Dion is scheduled to perform a series of 26 concerts over the next eight months. The City of Light buzzed with anticipation for the singer's comeback, with signs dotting the length of the Champs-Élysées and the famed river Seine.

Céline mania in Paris ahead of Canadian star's sold-out comeback tour

card_3.headline: New statues added to controversial Prime Minister's Path in Wilmot, Ont.
card_3.article_content:
Four statues of former Canadian leaders were added to the Prime Minister's Path project in Wilmot, Ont., on Saturday. Not everyone was pleased.

The contested project, now run by Createscape Waterloo Region, held an afternoon unveiling with the leadership of Wilmot Township at a municipal park by Castle Kilbride in Baden, a small community west of Kitchener.

"Obviously we're very happy that [the project] has found its footing once again," Don Bourgeois, chair of the board and president of Createscape Waterloo Region, told CBC News.

"Our purpose is to help create public art that has that emotional attachment, but also gets people... to have discussion about the future of Canada, the history of Canada, of art and what art is about."

The four new statues depict Sir John Abbott, Sir John Thompson, Sir Mackenzie Bowell and Sir Charles Tupper. They join statues of Sir John A. Macdonald, Kim Campbell, Sir Robert Borden, William Lyon Mackenzie King and Lester B. Pearson.
