Around a dozen protesters attended, decrying the project as insensitive and poorly conceived.

Wilmot Township moves forward with Prime Ministers Path project

Don Bourgeois, chair of the board and president of Createscape Waterloo Region, stands beside a statue of Lester B. Pearson. Bourgeois said the project is returning with an educational component to provide context behind each prime minister. (John Dalusong/CBC)

The Prime Ministers Path project was first proposed in 2013. The project aimed to honour former Canadian leaders with 22 bronze statues placed in a park to celebrate Canada's 150th birthday.

The project faced controversy from the beginning, however, with Kitchener councillors rejecting the idea of having the statues at Victoria Park in 2014 and Waterloo's Wilfrid Laurier University backing out of the agreement to put the statues at the school in 2016.

The statues would later find a home at Castle Kilbride in the village of Baden that same year.

By 2020, the statue of Sir John A. Macdonald was put in storage after a public call for it to be removed for his role in the residential school system. The project was then cancelled by the township's council in 2021, leading to the removal of the statues.

A protester holds up a sign that says, 'take away John. A' in Baden, Ont., on Sep. 12, 2026. Behind the protester is Sir John A. Macdonald's statue. (John Dalusong/CBC)

Last April, Wilmot council voted to proceed with the project. The vote involved giving Createscape Waterloo Region custody of the nine statues it owns, as well as entering into an agreement with the group to display the statues in municipal parkland for the next 20 years.

Work underway to re-install Prime Ministers Path in Wilmot Township

Createscape shares its plans for Prime Ministers Path in Wilmot

The project now includes an added educational component, with the Six Nations of the Grand River playing an important role, Bourgeois said.

"The Six Nations [of the Grand River] will be involved in making sure that our website, which will include historical educational materials, reflects the issues that resulted from decisions of the prime ministers over the last century and a half," he said.

But the addition of an educational component is not enough, said Benny Skinner, who uses they/them pronouns, and led Saturday's protest.

"If you actually take the time to learn about the prime ministers, the history of who they are and what they've done, and you learn proper authentic history that includes Indigenous peoples history, what you'll realize is that this is an extremely insensitive and poorly thought-out project," they said.

The project has been criticized as insensitive to Indigenous people since its inception.

When Wilfrid Laurier University declined to host the statues in 2016, opponents of the project said there had been insufficient consultation and celebrating the country's past prime ministers would be culturally insensitive given the university is built on land that traditionally belonged to Indigenous people.

Wilmot's Prime Ministers Path will continue, but now as a community-led project

Bourgeois insists that Indigenous perspectives have been taken into account.

"They were included in a sense right from the beginning, that issue with respect to how Canada, through the prime ministers' leadership, have dealt with First Nations was part of the discussion," Bourgeois explained.

"But clearly, we failed to communicate that properly. We failed to do it in a fashion that was sufficiently collaborative."

That has changed, he said: "Today, thankfully, we're down on a different path."

Benny Skinner (pictured) said Indigenous perspectives were not sufficiently reflected in the renewed Prime Ministers Path project. Don Bourgeois of Createscape said the involvement of Six Nations of the Grand River will help address concerns. (John Dalusong/CBC)

But Skinner, who was co-lead for the consultancy the last time there was a community engagement for the project, said concerns raised during consultations were not heeded.

"They're looking for an Indigenous person to check off that it's fine so that they can continue to do this project the way that it is," Skinner said.

"None of the Indigenous people I have spoken to, in the hundreds, about this project, want this project on these lands."

Sculptor Nathan Scott believes it is important to highlight all aspects of Canadian history. He sculpted the four newest statues in 2019, referring to them as "the unfortunate four" for what he sees as their limited achievements in office.

"I'm a proud Canadian. I love our history," he said. "It wasn't always done perfectly. It's the good, bad and sometimes there's ugliness to it, but it's who we are."

"And if we don't have history, if we try to erase it, who are we? Who are we at all?"

Nathan Scott rests his hand on his sculpture of Sir Robert Borden. Scott finished the newest statues in 2019, calling them 'the unfortunate four,' but was forced to hide them following backlash. (John Dalusong/CBC)

Future changes to the project could yet win over opponents, Skinner said. They proposed changing its name, moving it to a hidden area so people don't have to see it and better collaboration with Indigenous people.

For his part, Bourgeois said the educational aspect of the project will remain important. This includes hosting educational symposia where the history and work of each prime minister will be discussed.

For now, the long-term goal remains completing the remaining 13 statues, he said.

Though Canada has had 24 prime ministers, Justin Trudeau and Mark Carney won't be included in the current project — to avoid it becoming "a little bit too political," Bourgeois said.

card_4.headline: Swedish election could see far-right party join government for 1st time
card_4.article_content:
Swedes vote in an election on Sunday that will either bring a far-right party into government for ‌the first time or shift the country back towards the liberalism it has long been known for.

Sweden's centre-left opposition holds a narrow lead over the ruling right-wing bloc ahead of a Sept. 13 election for parliament, pointing to a likely change of government, several opinion polls have shown this week.

But Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who has trailed in opinion polls throughout his four years ​in office, has been catching up in the final weeks of campaigning, with rival Magdalena ​Andersson and her Social Democrats losing ground.

Supporters of the right-wing bloc say its policies have helped curb gang violence and cut immigration dramatically, and that a victory would amount to a public endorsement of that approach and more in ​the same vein in the years ahead.

"We can unify parties, voters and issues into joint action. That's why we ⁠get things done," Kristersson, who ⁠has pledged to bring the far-right Sweden Democrats into government if his bloc wins, ‌told reporters in parliament this week.

Magdalena Andersson of the centre-left Social Democrats, left, and Ulf Kristersson of Sweden's ruling right-wing bloc are seen before a televised debate in Gavle on Wednesday. (Anders Wiklund /TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

Critics counter that the agenda is undermining civil liberties while forcing immigrants to conform more closely to Swedish cultural norms or leave the country, urged on by both carrot and stick.

"We've become a harder society, a quieter society, but also a poorer society as we've had growth far below our potential and where households see their pay checks buy ⁠less and less," Andersson told Reuters.

Right-wing bloc wins narrow majority in Sweden, marking major political shift

"Our country has based its strength on sharing in each other's achievements and that we stick together when things are hard."

Polling stations in the EU member state of 10 million people, which joined NATO after Russia's full-scale invasion ‌of Ukraine, open at 8 a.m. local with exit polls due soon after they close at 8 p.m.

People line up outside a polling station in Stockholm on Friday. (Nicklas Thegerström/TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

Electoral success for the Sweden Democrats would be welcomed by Europe's rising far-right parties, boosted by a significant win in a German state election this month by the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany.

The right has already agreed to form a four-party government led by Kristersson if they win, while Andersson's ​path to power is more uncertain.

Far-right victory in German state expected to send shockwaves throughout the world

The election could ultimately be decided by whether the Liberals surpass the 4 per cent threshold to win seats in parliament, bolstering a right wing that includes Moderates, Christian Democrats and, since ⁠being invited by Kristersson earlier this year, Sweden Democrats.

The Sweden Democrats were founded in the 1980s by far-right extremists. Veteran politician Jimmie Åkesson took over the party in 2005, but until 2018, no party would have anything to do with them.

Sweden Democrats leader Jimmie Åkesson votes in Rinkeby, a suburb of Stockholm, on Saturday. (Claudio Bresciani/TT News Agency/The Associated Press)

The party's message that decades of overly generous immigration policies are behind a surge in shooting and gang crime has struck a chord with voters in recent years.

Since 2022, the Sweden Democrats have propped up Kristersson's government in parliament — building credibility with the broader right-wing bloc, despite not holding any cabinet positions — in exchange for policy concessions on immigration and policing.

Meanwhile, the rival blocs have converged on several voter priorities, including support for ⁠Ukraine, military ⁠rearmament and relief for households hit by the cost-of-living ​crisis.

Mamma mia! Contested Swedish cultural heritage list includes IKEA — but not ABBA

While the opposition Social Democrats, Greens, Left Party and Centre Party broadly agree on the need for higher welfare and public spending, divisions persist on many ​issues, including immigration, where Andersson's party wants ⁠a more restrictive line than some of its would-be partners.

They are also at odds over issues including a tax on billionaires and building new nuclear reactors, while the Centre refuses to support a government that includes the Left Party, increasing the challenge Andersson would face to form a cabinet.

Luring the Christian Democrats to switch camps to create a centrist government is favoured by the Centre Party, but so far looks a distant prospect.

card_5.headline: Canadian women improve to 3-0 at wheelchair basketball worlds in Ottawa with win over China
card_5.article_content:
Canada's women's wheelchair basketball team improved to 3-0 in the preliminary round at the world championships in Ottawa with a 66-62 win over China on Saturday at TD Place.

Veteran Kady Dandeneau of Pender Island, B.C., led the way once again with a game-high 37 points to go along with 10 rebounds and six assists while shooting 15-of-29 from the field. Arinn Young also delivered another strong performance for Canada with a triple double.

Young, from St. Albert, Alta., scored 19 points while adding 10 rebounds and 10 assists to help Canada secure the Group A win. The game was tied 30-30 at halftime and ultimately went down to the wire, as Canada only led 47-46 entering the final quarter following a clutch three-pointer from Dandeneau.

Young made a two-pointer with 1:10 left to play for a one-point lead and Dandeneau sealed the win in the final seconds, drawing a foul while scoring before hitting the ensuing free throw.

“Obviously, we’re really pumped about how we played and what our game plan was,” Canadian player Tara Llanes said in a press release. “Like in any game, you have some blips, but overall, I felt like our defence was strong, we made some good rotations and went out there, and Young and Dandeneau lit it up, so that’s what we need.”

Ottawa 2026 IWBF Women's Wheelchair Basketball World Championships: Canada vs. China

Lin Suiling led China (1-2) with 19 points and 12 assists, with Zhang Xuemei adding 18 points and 13 rebounds.

Canada shot 51 per cent (25/47) from the field and 30 per cent (3/10) from beyond the arc.

Canadian women rout Australia to claim 2nd win of wheelchair basketball worlds in Ottawa

Home court, high hopes as Canada's men and women chase wheelchair basketball world gold

China defeated Canada in the women's bronze-medal match at the 2024 Paralympics in Paris.

The Canadian women will next face Brazil on Sunday at 2:45 p.m. ET at TD Place before wrapping up their preliminary-round schedule against Great Britain at Carleton University on Tuesday at 2:30 p.m. ET.

“I think we just keep building on this,” Llanes added. “Mids and littles keep getting more into the action and being able to create some things, and I think we’ll be unstoppable.”

The United States and Paralympic champion Netherlands are also undefeated with 3-0 records in Group B.

The women's team opened their world-championship campaign with a 76-51 win over Spain on Wednesday before defeating Australia 79-30 on Thursday.

The Canadian men's team (2-1) had the day off because Iran, their scheduled opponents, had to withdraw from the tournament due to visa issues.
